records.themeTitle: Recognition at the opening of a blessing
records.themeSummary: The movement from direct address to concealment differs from an awareness permanently acquired in the heart.
records.explanation: Dover Tzedek explains the same change of grammatical person through the difference between an opening recognition and an enduring possession of the heart. Its preceding discussion describes that enduring possession as the completion of the stages of service. This gives the siman's moment of direct address a precise role: it begins and directs the act, even while the awareness is not yet continuously manifest. It also connects this to the initial intention discussed in Siman 5.
records.targetEnglish: Therefore, in this world, ‘I am not read as I am written’ (Pesachim 50a): every blessing begins in direct address, ‘Blessed are You,’ and then becomes concealed, ‘Who has sanctified us.’ Only at the beginning do ‘his eyes look directly ahead,’ as written in Tanya, chapter 41, that an intention for its own sake suffices at the beginning. [Therefore, a blessing adjoining another blessing needs only the first opening (Berakhot 46a). Some blessings conclude with ‘Blessed,’ corresponding to ‘its beginning is words of Torah and its end is words of Torah,’ explained above in another connection; this is not the place to elaborate.]

records.originEnglish: This also explains why all liturgical blessings open in the second-person direct address "Blessed are You...": for at the very start of the blessing, the Blessed Name must be directly present before one's eyes, as though He is standing over him and issuing the command. Yet the conclusion transitions into the third person "...Who has sanctified us", because He immediately recedes into transcendence, as it is written: "Over its fledglings He hovers" (Deuteronomy 32:11) — touching yet not touching, as is well known in mystical thought.

records.themeTitle: Why the smaller light serves the search
records.themeSummary: Concealment leaves room for the person's own work of bringing light into particular hidden places.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef explains why the candle, rather than the larger torch, suits the search of the heart. A place where the light is already seen as complete leaves no apparent deficiency for human work to address. The candle represents the person's deliberate effort to recognize and reveal holiness within the concealed particulars. This clarifies why the siman values a mitzvah's limited light precisely during darkness, while still requiring a search as far as one's ability reaches.
records.targetEnglish: This is their meaning: one does not search by the light of a torch, but by a candle, which is suited to searching. Hashem concealed His light so that there are places in this world where His light is not recognizable; these are called ‘holes and cracks.’ Through his labor and service, called a candle, a person brings the honor of Heaven even there, as it is written, ‘The soul of a person is Hashem's candle’ (Proverbs 20:27). The righteous stand before the Shechinah like a candle before a torch. This is Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's reasoning: the candle can be brought into holes and cracks. Hashem established His will that there should, as it were, be holes and cracks in this world: to human eyes, light and goodness seem absent there and the honor of Heaven seems deficient. This leaves a place for human labor, through which a person, serving Hashem with his own effort, illuminates those holes and cracks, fills them with the shining of his candle, and completes the work so that no breach remains and His honor is whole, without deficiency. This is the candle suited to searching. From the standpoint of the torch, however, there is no place for human service.

records.originEnglish: And 'inside his house' means within the inner chambers of his heart, where candlelight is ideal for inspection: searching out the leaven in the dough hidden within holes and cracks is accomplished far better at night during darkness, when candlelight shines brightly unlike daytime when a lamp in broad daylight yields no benefit (Chullin 60b), and see Yerushalmi Pesachim 1:1 that by day even in a dark chamber a candle does not illuminate well; for when the Divine Name is fully manifest over the micro-cosmos, the candle of an isolated mitzvah is eclipsed, and through this inspection one can purge all subtle souring impurities from the crevices of the heart as far as human reach extends, nullifying whatever remains in his heart.

records.themeTitle: What makes a descent a preparation
records.themeSummary: The later discussion names the response that turns darkness toward renewed Torah: recognition and a cry to Hashem.
records.explanation: Siman 151 returns to the very cloud-and-rain teaching quoted here, but spells out the human response: a person recognizes his decline and cries out. Its example of Refidim before Sinai explains preparation through renewed need for Torah. This adds a practical distinction to the cloud image without erasing the present siman's qualification that rain is beneficial in its proper season.
records.targetEnglish: The times of descent a person experiences, when he has no desire for light and divine service, are a preparation for a great ascent. This comes through the cry he cries when he considers his ways and sees his lowliness and descent. As it is written, ‘They journeyed from Refidim and came to the wilderness of Sinai’ (Exodus 19:2): the Sages' exposition of ‘Refidim’ is known—that their hands had weakened in words of Torah (Sanhedrin 106a). This was a preparation for the giving of the Torah, the ultimate strengthening of the hands in words of Torah.

records.themeTitle: Alacrity begins with preparation
records.themeSummary: Et HaOchel explains the siman's explicit cross-reference and preserves the distinction between readiness and hurried appetite.
records.explanation: The siman expressly refers the reader to Et HaOchel. There, the word ‘enter’ is explained as preparation even for an ordinary meal, and all the more for eating terumah or a Shabbat meal. This distinguishes promptly beginning the mitzvah's preparation from consuming its food impulsively. The quotation retains the closing qualification: the instruction to ‘snatch and eat’ concerns a person whose settled attention is already in Torah and service.
records.targetEnglish: The second counsel is deliberateness. The foundation of overpowering appetite is haste: a person wants to swallow and satisfy his desire quickly. As stated in Beitzah 25b, planting ‘cuts off the feet’ of butchers and those who have relations with menstruating women—the two principal desires mentioned, which arise from haste. The Sages said in Chullin 84a that the Torah teaches proper conduct: a person should eat meat only with preparation. At the beginning of Berakhot (2a–b), the Sages use ‘enters’ and ‘enter’ for every meal mentioned, teaching that eating requires an entrance and preparation. Even for a poor person's meal they say ‘enters’ (see Tosafot there, beginning ‘From the time,’ and my novellae there). Likewise, eating terumah and eating on Shabbat, which are mitzvah meals, are described as ‘entering’: they require preparation, rather than casual eating like a glutton who snatches and eats. As for ‘snatch and eat’ in Eruvin 54a, it appears that people differ: someone whose thoughts are already firmly attached to words of Torah may snatch and eat, like someone at a wedding feast whose main concern is the celebration and who eats incidentally. There is no concern or suspicion about his heart's appetite, and one can be confident that his thoughts are attached only to Torah and service.
records.originHebrew: וְתַנָּא דִידַן: "נִכְנָסִין", לְאוֹרוֹיֵי דְּכֹהֲנִים זְרִיזִים וּזְרִיזִים מַקְדִּימִין, וְתֵיכֶף בְּרֶגַע רִאשׁוֹנָה שֶׁמְּטוֹהָרִים הֵם נִכְנָסִים, שֶׁמִּיָּד בְּהַגִּיעַ זְמַן הַמִּצְוָה יַתְחִיל הַכְּנִיסָה וְהַהַכָנָה לַמִּצְוָה. וַאֲגַב אוֹרְחָא קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן דְּצָרִיךְ כְּנִיסָה וְהַכָנָה לַמִּצְוָה וְלֹא אוֹכְלִין מִיָּד.
records.originEnglish: Our Tanna uses the term "enter" (nikhnasin) to teach that priests are zealous and the zealous act early: at the very first moment they are purified they enter, teaching that the instant a mitzvah's time arrives, one must begin the entrance and preparation for it. Incidental to this, we learn that every mitzvah requires entrance and preparation, rather than eating immediately.

records.targetRef: Sod Yesharim, The Eighth Day of Pesach 3:1
records.themeTitle: A share in certain holiness through service amid doubt
records.themeSummary: The second festival day allows human participation in the holiness of the first day.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim uses the same example of the second festival day to explain why service arising from doubt has positive spiritual content. The added observance gives Israel a share, through its own willing effort, in the first day's certain holiness. In the full discourse this follows the example of declaring a firstborn animal holy even though it is holy from birth. The comparison concerns the established observance named by the siman; it does not settle which blessing to recite in other doubtful cases.
records.targetEnglish: The reading of this passage on the second festival day in the Diaspora, which also arises on account of doubt, points to this as well. It teaches that through what Israel adds because of doubt, with generosity and willing hearts, they have a share even in the holiness of the first day. Its holiness is certain, like holiness rooted at the source; nevertheless, Israel acquires a share in it through the labor of their own hands.

records.targetRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume II, Genesis, Bereshit 5
records.themeTitle: Compassion as an awakening from below
records.themeSummary: The correspondence between human and heavenly action includes a parent's mercy toward a child who has strayed.
records.explanation: Mei HaShiloach places the principle of awakening from below within the structure of human family life. A parent's compassionate intercession for a disobedient child awakens corresponding compassion Above. This supplies a concrete ethical example for the siman's general principle, alongside its examples of Torah discussed below and spoken Above. The source presents the relation through measure-for-measure judgment.
records.targetEnglish: Therefore Hashem arranged for creation to multiply through birth from a father and mother, and established compassion in parents' hearts. Even if their children transgress their parents' will and commands, and even intend to anger them, He nevertheless implanted compassion in the parents' hearts so that they will still ask Hashem not to punish their children. For it is the nature of a cause to have mercy on what proceeds from it; its compassion rises above everything and covers all transgressions. This requires, measure for measure, that Hashem have compassion on Israel even when they transgress His will, according to the rule of justice, measure for measure.

records.themeTitle: What to ask when attention is constrained
records.themeSummary: The short prayer can ask for wider understanding when one cannot fully clarify a particular request.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef reads the same exchange with Eliyahu as a difficulty in clarifying one's request: under distraction, a person cannot adequately examine whether the desired benefit could burden someone else. The short prayer asks Hashem to raise the petitioner's understanding toward the source of the good. This gives positive content to the siman's preference for a short prayer that can be said with attention.
records.targetEnglish: He said to him, ‘You should have prayed a short prayer.’ For when goodness proceeds directly from Hashem, there is no suffering in that goodness, as it is written, ‘Evil does not dwell with You’ (Psalms 5:5), expounded in the Midrash (Tanchuma, Tazria): evil does not descend from Heaven. Only when goodness descends clothed in the garments of this world can it appear to a person that he suffers from that goodness. A person must therefore see that no one suffers because of his good fortune. When he is distracted and cannot clarify himself in this way, the counsel is to pray a short prayer. Concerning the short prayer, the Gemara later states (Berakhot 29b): ‘Others say: The needs of Your people are many, and their understanding is limited.’ The entire prayer concerns their limited understanding: they pray to Hashem to raise their perception. They will then receive the goodness from its source and have no suffering. When a person sees that he receives goodness from its source, he has no suffering. This is the counsel when a person is distracted: to pray that Hashem raise his perception to the source, so that he will have no suffering.

records.targetRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Toldot 9
records.themeTitle: The field's expansion takes its character from its direction
records.themeSummary: Mei HaShiloach distinguishes expansion in unholy desires from Yaakov's expansion in holiness.
records.explanation: Mei HaShiloach explicitly interprets ‘field’ as an expansion of desire, then distinguishes Esav's field from Yaakov's field blessed by Hashem. This helps identify the kind of expansion intended by the siman: its claim that bodily desires are uncommon concerns the spiritual state under discussion. The word ‘field’ by itself does not always signify freedom from bodily desire. This is a conceptual comparison, rather than an identification of the unnamed teaching Rav Tzadok reports hearing.
records.targetEnglish: ‘See, the fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a field,’ and so forth. A field alludes to an expansion of desires. Esav was therefore called ‘a man of the field,’ because he expanded into all kinds of evil cravings and desires. Yaakov our father, however, had an expansion in holiness. This is ‘like the fragrance of a field that Hashem has blessed’—the holy apple orchard.

records.themeTitle: The heart's understanding and its expression
records.themeSummary: A reason's inward force is not transferred intact merely by stating it.
records.explanation: Resisei Layla distinguishes the reasons a sage can disclose from the inward taste of those reasons in the heart. Speech bears an impression of that understanding but does not reproduce it completely. This explains why the present siman demands a further clarification when a private conviction becomes public speech or action. The comparison preserves both sides: inward understanding has substance, while the speaker's certainty alone does not establish the matter for others.
records.targetEnglish: ‘Faces’ means disclosures: the sage shows the grounds for saying what he says. The forty-nine are known to be seven times seven, corresponding to the seven attributes of the structure of revelation. The fiftieth gate corresponds to understanding in the heart: one cannot disclose to another the heart's feeling, the inward taste one feels concerning a matter, for that taste cannot be explained and disclosed. This is as they said in Sanhedrin 35a, ‘The human heart forgets’: it cannot be disclosed in writing, nor can it be disclosed in speech. Rather, the impression in the heart clothes itself in speech. The force of the speech follows the feeling of the reason's taste in the heart, and the heart's feeling can be recognized in the speech; but the actual taste that one feels cannot be disclosed.

records.themeTitle: Creation reaches beyond an improved surface
records.themeSummary: Another discussion of the same verse illustrates transformation through effort, Torah, and heavenly mercy.
records.explanation: Ohr Zarua LaTzadik also reads ‘Create in me a pure heart’ as creation from nothing. Its context is Rabbi Akiva's transformation through Torah and effort, followed by the images of a convert as newly born and flesh restored like a child's. This gives the siman's final remedy a concrete meaning: prayer for mercy can seek a renewed spiritual beginning, rather than treating one's present condition as an unchangeable verdict. The matching cross-reference is suggestive; it does not by itself prove which passage the author intended by ‘elsewhere.’
records.targetEnglish: Thus, since he [Rabbi Akiva] was descended from converts, through his effort he became holy flesh and an Israelite soul. Previously he had been unlearned and said, ‘If only I had a Torah scholar,’ and so forth (Pesachim 49b): his natural starting point was not good. Only through effort did he merit the Oral Torah, which clarifies that the essential thing is to be of Israel's holy stock; through his effort he brought it about that he belonged to that holy stock. [Effort is effective even in this, and Hashem has many means, as stated in Taanit 25a: ‘Am I asking from someone who does not have it?’ The principal means is Torah, as the Midrash teaches in several places concerning Yitro and his descendants. A person can attain heavenly mercy so that ‘his flesh returns like the flesh of a young child’ (II Kings 5:14), like a convert who converts, who is considered a newborn child (Yevamot 22a), and return to holy flesh. This is as I wrote elsewhere on ‘Create in me a pure heart, God’ (Psalms 51:12): as is known, ‘creation’ everywhere denotes something from nothing. These matters contain great and substantial discussions, whose place is not here.]

records.themeTitle: The first commandment leaves a beginning for return
records.themeSummary: The priority of Anokhi also means that a person need not complete all repair before beginning a mitzvah.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef draws another consequence from the same order of commandments. If removal of evil were an absolute precondition for every positive act, someone not yet purified would have no beginning. Anokhi comes first as divine kindness that leaves repentance and mitzvot open even while repair remains incomplete. This complements the siman's account of faith leading to protection; it does not turn unfinished repair into permission to continue the wrongdoing.
records.targetEnglish: He explained that this was among Hashem's kindnesses. If the statement ‘You shall have no other gods,’ which signifies turning from evil, had preceded ‘I am,’ which signifies doing good, then someone not yet clean in turning from evil would have no place to perform any mitzvah, because he was not yet purified in turning from evil. Hashem's saying ‘I am’ first teaches that even if someone has, Heaven forbid, stumbled in something bad, repentance is not withheld from him, and he can perform mitzvot even while he is not yet clean in turning from evil.

records.themeTitle: What the prophets reject in a mechanical offering
records.themeSummary: The commanded act has a purpose: the refinement and divine will expressed through it.
records.explanation: Kometz HaMinchah directly addresses the apparent contradiction behind the siman's sacrificial analogy: the prophets speak of offerings as unrequested although the Torah commands them. The criticism concerns making the external act an isolated final purpose. Its intended refinement and relation to Hashem's will give the act its meaning. This clarifies the siman's emphasis on the desire to pray while preserving the distinction between that purpose and the existence of a commandment.
records.targetEnglish: A person should not set his final purpose and intention on a particular thing, such as restraining desires, studying Torah, engaging in service, or the like. Concerning this the prophet repeatedly cries out that sacrifices were not requested. The commentators ask: were they not in fact commanded? The meaning is that they made this alone the final purpose—to bring sacrifices and perform mitzvot—as it is written, ‘Their fear of Me became a commandment of people learned by rote’ (Isaiah 29:13); this was not commanded. As the Midrash says (Tanchuma, Shemini 8; Bereshit Rabbah 44:1): what difference does it make to the Holy One, blessed be He, whether one slaughters from the neck, and so forth? Rather, the purpose is to refine. The bare physical act is not the final purpose of the command; its purpose is what each mitzvah signifies and intends, in order to refine.

records.themeTitle: The beginning matters when judging compulsion
records.themeSummary: An overpowering later inclination does not by itself disclose the character of the whole course of conduct.
records.explanation: Kometz HaMinchah examines the same Talmudic case of initial compulsion followed by apparent willingness. It directs attention back to the beginning, then offers Torah's restoring light as another reading of the prophetic passage. This illuminates why the siman combines recognition of genuine compulsion with its explicit refusal to let a person certify that condition for himself. The parallel supplies a distinction to examine, rather than a ruling about any particular case.
records.targetEnglish: ‘Their ear is uncircumcised, and they cannot listen’ (Jeremiah 6:10)—even if they wish to, so that they are like people under compulsion; for ‘Hashem's word has become a reproach to them; they do not desire it’ (there). This is like ‘its beginning was under compulsion and its end with willingness’ (Ketubot 51b): according to Shmuel's father, ‘the inclination clothed her.’ So too with the inclination to idolatry then, as Menashe said (Sanhedrin 102b): at the end, even the willingness is compulsion; the essential matter is the beginning. Or it may be understood according to the saying (Yerushalmi Chagigah 1:7), ‘Would that they abandoned Me but kept My Torah: its light would return them to the good,’ and as stated (Kiddushin 30b), ‘I created the evil inclination; I created Torah as its remedy.’
records.originHebrew: אֲבָל הָאָדָם עַצְמוֹ אֵינוֹ יָכוֹל לְהָעִיד עַל עַצְמוֹ בָּזֶה, כִּי אוּלַי עֲדַיִן הָיָה לוֹ כֹּחַ לִכְפּוֹת הַיֵּצֶר וּכְמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי בָּזֶה מֵעִנְיַן זִמְרִי שֶׁטָּעָה בָּזֶה]:
records.originEnglish: However, a person cannot testify about himself in this regard, for perhaps he still possessed sufficient strength to master the inclination as I heard concerning the episode of Zimri who erred in this very self-assessment.
records.targetHebrew: "הִנֵּה עֲרֵלָה אָזְנָם וְלֹא יוּכְלוּ לְהַקְשִׁיב" [יִרְמְיָהוּ ו׳:י׳] — גַּם אִם יִרְצוּ, וְהֵם כַּאֲנוּסִים; כִּי "הִנֵּה דְבַר ה' הָיָה לָהֶם לְחֶרְפָּה לֹא יַחְפְּצוּ בוֹ" [שָׁם]. כְּמוֹ "תְּחִלָּתוֹ בְּאֹנֶס וְסוֹפוֹ בְּרָצוֹן" (כְּתֻבּוֹת נ״א עַמּוּד ב׳): לַאֲבוּהּ דִּשְׁמוּאֵל — "יִצְרָא אַלְבְּשַׁהּ", וְכֵן אָז — יִצְרָא דַעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר מְנַשֶּׁה [סַנְהֶדְרִין ק״ב עַמּוּד ב׳], וּבַסּוֹף גַּם רָצוֹן אֹנֶס, רַק הָעִקָּר עַל הַתְּחִלָּה. אוֹ יֵאָמֵר עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (יְרוּשַׁלְמִי חֲגִיגָה פֶּרֶק א׳ הֲלָכָה ז׳): "הַלְוַאי אוֹתִי עָזָבוּ וְתוֹרָתִי שָׁמָרוּ, הַמָּאוֹר שֶׁבָּהּ יַחֲזִירֵם לְמוּטָב"; וּכְמַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב (קִדּוּשִׁין ל׳ עַמּוּד ב׳): "בָּרָאתִי יֵצֶר הָרָע — בָּרָאתִי לוֹ תּוֹרָה תַּבְלִין".

records.targetRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Lech Lecha 7
records.themeTitle: Sincere intention does not remove the meaning of association
records.themeSummary: Mei HaShiloach applies the same verse to avoiding an appearance of joining another's wrongful purpose.
records.explanation: Mei HaShiloach applies ‘Do not walk in the way with them’ to David's association with Achish. Even an inward intention for Heaven does not remove the need to prevent others from reasonably reading the association as participation in their purpose. This adds a distinct outward dimension to the siman's warning about joining a wicked partner for an apparently good end. The full source also examines removing personal benefit, rather than treating intention alone as sufficient clarification.
records.targetEnglish: So too with King David, who went with Achish king of Gat (I Samuel 29–30) and did not wish to benefit from the spoil, for this too was contrary to proper judgment. Although he did not share their intention—his intention was for Heaven—it nevertheless says, ‘Do not walk in the way with them’ (Proverbs 1:15). That is: even when you are not inwardly going with them, refrain from them in such a way that others cannot mistakenly think you are going with them.
records.originHebrew: מח] לֹא יִתְחַבֵּר עִם רְשָׁעִים, וַאֲפִילּוּ לַעֲשׂוֹת מִצְוָה, וְכֵן הוּא מְפוֹרָשׁ בַּמְּכִילְתָּא, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "בְּהִתְחַבֶּרְךָ עִם אֲחַזְיָהוּ פָּרַץ ה' אֶת מַעֲשֶׂיךָ]" (דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים ב כ, לז), וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁנִּתְחַבֵּר עִמּוֹ לִלְחוֹם נֶגֶד אֲרָם. וְנֶאֱמַר: "בְּנִי, אַל תֵּלֵךְ בְּדֶרֶךְ אִתָּם" (מִשְׁלֵי א, טו), וּבְכָל מָקוֹם "דֶּרֶךְ" בְּסֵפֶר מִשְׁלֵי רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר דֶּרֶךְ הַתּוֹרָה וְהַמִּצְווֹת.
records.originEnglish: One must not join with the wicked, even to perform a mitzvah; and this is explicitly taught in the Mekhilta, as written: "Because you have joined with Ahaziah, Hashem has destroyed your works" (II Chronicles 20:37), even though he joined with him to wage war against Aram. And Scripture warns: "My son, walk not in the way with them" (Proverbs 1:15), and everywhere the word "way" (derekh) in Proverbs signifies the path of Torah and commandments.
records.targetHebrew: וְכֵן הָעִנְיָן בְּדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ שֶׁהָלַךְ עִם אָכִישׁ מֶלֶךְ גַּת (שְׁמוּאֵל א, כט–ל), שֶׁלֹּא רָצָה לֵהָנוֹת מֵהַשָּׁלָל, כִּי גַּם זֹאת הָיְתָה נֶגֶד הַמִּשְׁפָּט, כִּי אַף שֶׁלֹּא הָלַךְ בְּכַוָּונָתָם כִּי כַּוָּונָתוֹ הָיְתָה לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם, אַךְ נֶאֱמַר (מִשְׁלֵי א, טו): "אַל תֵּלֵךְ בְּדֶרֶךְ אִתָּם", הַיְינוּ אַף שֶׁאֵין אַתָּה הוֹלֵךְ עִמָּם, מִכָּל מָקוֹם תִּמָּנַע מֵהֶם בְּאוֹפֶן שֶׁלֹּא יוּכְלוּ לִטְעוֹת עָלֶיךָ שֶׁאַתָּה הוֹלֵךְ אִתָּם.

records.targetRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayetzei 6
records.themeTitle: What the stumbling can restore
records.themeSummary: The return after failure can bring Torah into the heart with a stronger desire than before.
records.explanation: Mei HaShiloach reads Hashem's promise to return Yaakov as both the restoration of something lost and teshuvah. The same statement about learning through stumbling is explained through an increased desire that brings the Torah into the heart. This identifies a positive result of the repair described here: a deeper attachment to the very Torah in which one stumbled. The subject is the return from a stumbling that occurred, not an instruction to seek one.
records.targetEnglish: The Holy One, blessed be He, then showed him the clarifications and suffering he would still need to undergo, and promised him concerning them, ‘I will guard you wherever you go and return you to this land.’ ‘I will return you’ is an expression of restoring a lost thing. For a person does not truly grasp words of Torah unless he has stumbled in them (Gittin 43a): through the stumbling that happens to a person, the words of Torah enter his heart with a greater desire than before. This is ‘I will return you’—an expression of teshuvah.
records.originHebrew: וְעַל כָּזֶה אָמְרוּ (גִּטִּין מג.): אֵין אָדָם עוֹמֵד עַל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן נִכְשַׁל, שֶׁעַל יְדֵי הַמַּכְשֵׁלָה הוּא מֵבִין שֶׁלְּכָךְ נוֹצַר – לְתַקֵּן אוֹתוֹ דָּבָר.
records.originEnglish: And concerning this they said (Gittin 43a): "A person does not truly master words of Torah unless he has stumbled in them," meaning that through the stumbling he understands that for this purpose was he created: to rectify that specific thing.
records.targetHebrew: וְהֶרְאָה לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא אָז הַבֵּירוּרִין שֶׁיִּצְטָרֵךְ עוֹד לְהִתְבָּרֵר וְלִסְבּוֹל, וְעַל זֶה הִבְטִיחַ לוֹ "וּשְׁמַרְתִּיךָ בְּכֹל אֲשֶׁר תֵּלֵךְ וַהֲשִׁיבוֹתִיךָ אֶל הָאֲדָמָה הַזֹּאת", וַהֲשִׁיבוֹתִיךָ הוּא לְשׁוֹן הֲשָׁבַת אֲבֵידָה, כִּי אֵין אָדָם עוֹמֵד עַל דִּבְרֵי תּוֹרָה אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן נִכְשַׁל בָּהֶם (גִּיטִּין מֵם גִּימֶל עַמּוּד אָלֶף), וְהַיְינוּ כִּי עַל יְדֵי הַמִּכְשׁוֹל שֶׁבָּא לָאָדָם יִכָּנְסוּ הַדִּבְרֵי תּוֹרָה בְּלֵב הָאָדָם בְּחֵשֶׁק גָּדוֹל יוֹתֵר מִמִּקֹּדֶם, וְזֶהוּ "וַהֲשִׁיבוֹתִיךָ" הַיְינוּ לְשׁוֹן תְּשׁוּבָה.

records.targetRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Chayei Sarah 4
records.themeTitle: The answer already being prepared
records.themeSummary: Yitzchak's prayer and Rivkah's arrival illustrate help arranged before the request reaches expression.
records.explanation: Mei HaShiloach applies ‘Before they call, I answer’ to Yitzchak: Avraham has already sent his servant while Yitzchak is only now becoming inwardly ready to ask. His prayer and the arrival of the answer meet. This illustrates the siman's account of anticipatory help through an actual biblical narrative. The passage does not make the timing of an immediate answer a test of another petitioner's worth.
records.targetEnglish: ‘Yitzchak had come from coming,’ and so forth; ‘Yitzchak went out to converse,’ and so forth; ‘he saw, and behold,’ and so forth. Yitzchak was the root of all forms of fear in the world, even in refraining from action, as it is written, ‘He dwelt in the land of the Negev’—dried of every craving. Avraham our father recognized this quality in Yitzchak's soul and knew his great fear of taking any positive action, so he sent his servant to arrange a match for him. In truth, this was from Hashem, for the time had come for Yitzchak our father to marry. Yitzchak too began to awaken inwardly to ‘He did not create it for emptiness,’ and so forth. Yet because he feared taking practical action, he went out to converse in the field and pray that Hashem help him and bring him his match, for there is a person whose match comes to him (Moed Katan 18b). He was answered immediately in his prayer: ‘He raised his eyes,’ and so forth, for ‘Before they call, I answer.’
records.originHebrew: וַ"אֲחִישֶׁנָּה" הַיְינוּ "טֶרֶם יִקְרָאוּ", שֶׁמַּקְדִּים רְפוּאָה לַמַּכָּה.
records.originEnglish: Whereas "I will hasten it" corresponds to "Before they call I will answer" (Isaiah 65:24), wherein He prepares the cure prior to the blow.
records.targetHebrew: וְיִצְחָק בָּא מִבּוֹא וְכוּלֵי וַיֵּצֵא יִצְחָק לָשׂוּחַ וְכוּלֵי וַיַּרְא וְהִנֵּה וְכוּלֵי. הַיְינוּ כִּי יִצְחָק הָיָה שֹׁרֶשׁ לְכָל הַיִּרְאוֹת שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם אַף בְּשֵׁב וְאַל תַּעֲשֶׂה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב "וְהוּא יוֹשֵׁב בְּאֶרֶץ הַנֶּגֶב" הַיְינוּ מְנֻגָּב מִכָּל חֶמְדָּה, לָזֹאת אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ שֶׁהִכִּיר אֶת נֶפֶשׁ יִצְחָק בָּזֶה וְיָדַע כִּי מְאֹד נִמְצָא בּוֹ יִרְאָה לַעֲשׂוֹת אֵיזֶה מַעֲשֶׂה בְּקוּם וַעֲשֵׂה, שָׁלַח הוּא אֶת עַבְדּוֹ לְזַוֵּג לוֹ זִוּוּג. אַךְ בֶּאֱמֶת מֵאֵת הַשֵּׁם הָיְתָה זֹּאת, כִּי בָא הָעֵת שֶׁיִּשָּׂא יִצְחָק אָבִינוּ אִשָּׁה, וְגַם יִצְחָק הִתְחִיל לְהִתְעוֹרֵר בְּלִבּוֹ "לֹא תֹהוּ בְרָאָהּ" וְכוּלֵי, אַךְ בְּיַעַן שֶׁהָיָה יָרֵא לַעֲשׂוֹת אֵיזֶה מַעֲשֶׂה בְּפֹעַל לָזֹאת יָצָא לָשׂוּחַ בַּשָּׂדֶה וּלְהִתְפַּלֵּל לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁיַּעְזְרוֹ בָּזֶה וְיַזְמִין לוֹ זִוּוּגוֹ, כִּי יֵשׁ שֶׁזִּוּוּגוֹ בָּא אֶצְלוֹ (מוֹעֵד קָטָן יוֹד חֵית עַמּוּד בֵּית) וּמִיָּד נַעֲנָה בִּתְפִלָּתוֹ "וַיִּשָּׂא עֵינָיו" וְכוּלֵי כִּי "טֶרֶם יִקְרָאוּ וַאֲנִי אֶעֱנֶה".

records.targetRef: Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, The Egyptian Exile 6:11
records.themeTitle: The name preserves a beginning that calls for remembrance
records.themeSummary: The corresponding discussion of Egypt describes Torah knowledge as hidden and forgotten, awaiting renewal.
records.explanation: Ohr Zarua LaTzadik develops the same name-of-Israel argument through the generation in Egypt and the same case of a captive child or convert. Its concluding description is significant: Torah knowledge is hidden in the heart, forgotten, and needs to be recalled. This helps explain what the siman means by the sufficiency of the name as a foundation of belonging, while the cited case itself continues to recognize obligations and the need to learn them.
records.targetEnglish: The difference was only in the point within the heart. As the Sages said (Vayikra Rabbah 32:5), they were redeemed on account of four things. The intent of all four is that they distinguished themselves as a people of their own and called themselves ‘Israel.’ Even though no other distinguishing sign was visible, merely bearing the name and being set apart from the peoples by that name alone sufficed. [Therefore the book begins, ‘These are the names of the children of Israel’: this distinction of the name ‘children of Israel’ alone is the foundation of the Torah.] As the Sages stated at the beginning of the chapter Kelal Gadol (Shabbat 68b), even a child taken captive among the nations and a convert who converted among the nations is called someone who knew the fundamental principle of Shabbat and forgot it. So too with all Israel in Egypt then: because they were distinguished as a people of their own, although in practice ‘these worship idols,’ and so forth, they were considered to know the fundamental principle of Torah in the point within the heart. Knowledge of Torah lay hidden within them; it was merely forgotten and needed to be recalled.

records.themeTitle: Why an inward connection still needs a visible reminder
records.themeSummary: Tzitzit bring a concealed connection into conscious service and choice.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef places the same Midrash about the wood gatherer within the dispute with Korach. Israel's connection to divine light at its root does not dispense with practical reminders: concealment makes conscious return through a mitzvah necessary. This develops the siman's distinction between already knowing the command in the mind and remembering it actively in the heart. The reminder awakens a present response, rather than supplying a previously unknown prohibition.
records.targetEnglish: The mitzvah of tzitzit points to this, as stated in Tanna Devei Eliyahu: tzitzit was given after the sin of the wood gatherer. Its words are: The Holy One, blessed be He, said to Moshe, ‘Why did this man profane Shabbat?’ Moshe said before Him, ‘Master of the world, I do not know.’ The Holy One, blessed be He, said, ‘I will tell you. Throughout the six weekdays an Israelite has tefillin on his head and arm; he sees them and turns back from his deeds. But on Shabbat, when he has no tefillin, he therefore profaned Shabbat.’ The Holy One, blessed be He, said, ‘Go and choose for them a mitzvah practiced also on Shabbat and festivals’—this is tzitzit, and so forth. This indicates why Hashem gave Israel tzitzit: it is true that at their root they are encompassed by His light. But because Hashem desires human service, He established the possibility of a person stepping outward and experiencing a concealed place. Through tzitzit one brings forth the precious from the worthless: the person serving Hashem brings it out of concealment and returns before Hashem. He then has a share in the service, and the service is called by his name.

records.themeTitle: Examination after a mishap and the final clarification
records.themeSummary: A mishap can demand renewed clarification without proving that all earlier sincere service was severed from Hashem.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef examines the nazir who is unexpectedly defiled and begins to fear that his whole original undertaking was mistaken. It distinguishes that painful present examination from Hashem's final clarification, when the sincere intention and even its obstruction are shown as part of refinement. This adds a necessary distinction to the siman's inward examination after a stumbling: the demand to repair is real, while a person cannot turn his present misgivings into a complete verdict about the whole history of his service.
records.targetEnglish: These clarifications are very difficult and weighty for a person to undergo. They become ‘light’ in the World to Come, when Hashem will clarify all Israel's actions and illuminate them, showing that their actions had not been separated from His will, since in the depth of their hearts they intended them for Heaven. Even a person's good desire will not be lost; Hashem will join it to an act, as stated in Kiddushin 40a: if someone intended to perform a mitzvah and was prevented by circumstances beyond his control, Scripture credits him as though he performed it. Then it will become clear that even the obstruction occurred by His will. Since the person's whole aim, desire, and will were solely to fulfill His will, and God brought about the event preventing him, it follows that this too was for his benefit, refining him again and again. As the Midrash says (Tanchuma, Shemini): what difference does it make to the Holy One, blessed be He, whether one slaughters from the back of the neck or from the neck? Rather, it is to refine His creatures, as it is written, ‘Every word of Hashem is refined.’ All the concealments a person experienced—first thinking one order of service was good for him and afterward another—were only to refine him; he had never, Heaven forbid, been separated from His will.

records.themeTitle: Torah can renew the desire through which it is acquired
records.themeSummary: Veha'arev na asks for a sweetness that feeds further learning rather than ending in satiety.
records.explanation: Mei HaShiloach explains the very prayer cited here through a reciprocal movement: desire acquires Torah, and Torah in turn renews desire. Its interpretation of silver and gold distinguishes the energy of beginning from the need to keep that energy alive after acquiring knowledge. This explains why the siman's prayer for sweetness is part of the transition toward learning for its own sake, rather than a request for pleasantness detached from further service.
records.targetEnglish: This is also the meaning of the Gemara (Bava Metzia 44a): in his youth Rabbi taught his son Rabbi Shimon, ‘Silver acquires gold,’ and in his old age, ‘Gold acquires silver.’ In a person's youth there is great desire and longing for words of Torah, through which he acquires the gold: true words of Torah are called gold, while silver signifies desire and longing. In old age, however, a person must ask that his desire for words of Torah not depart, for all his powers of desire weaken. He therefore changed it to ‘Gold acquires silver’: this is a prayer to Hashem that words of Torah bring into his heart the desire for still more Torah. It is like a person already satisfied with food, who nevertheless desires to eat more when a good dish is brought before him. So it is with words of Torah. This is our daily prayer, ‘Hashem our God, please make the words of Your Torah sweet in our mouths’: that the Torah become sweet to us, so that we continually desire it more. This explains ‘You shall eat, eating and being satisfied’ (Joel 2:26): the doubled expression teaches that eating itself brings further desire. It is a parable for words of Torah, as explained.

records.themeTitle: Eliyahu's crisis redirects his prayer
records.themeSummary: The widow's loss calls Eliyahu toward intercession for the generation, even amid the miracles sustaining him.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef follows the same drought narrative into the death of the widow's son. It reads Eliyahu's distress as a summons to pray for the generation's repentance and the return of rain. This supplies a particular corrective within the siman's example: the miraculous assistance that sustained Eliyahu did not end the need to discern what Hashem desired next. The source directs his strength toward the life and return of the people.
records.targetEnglish: When Eliyahu saw the death of the widow of Tzarfat's son, it touched his very life. The child's mother argued that Eliyahu was responsible: because he had come to lodge with her, the Holy One, blessed be He, compared her deeds with Eliyahu's, recalled her sin, and she was punished. This event therefore touched Eliyahu's very life. He understood from Hashem's bringing about such an event that His will was for him to pray that the whole generation repent, so that rain should come after the famine had become so severe. Hashem desired Eliyahu to pray for the whole generation's repentance, for He does not desire the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from their ways and live. This is the Yerushalmi's meaning: when he revived the widow's son, the vow concerning dew and rain was released.

records.originEnglish: Behold, consider Elijah, concerning whom our Sages stated (Sanhedrin 113a) that the withholding of the rain was grievous before the Blessed Name; and nonetheless He commanded Elijah: "Go... and hide yourself, etc." (I Kings 17:3), miraculously assisting him to hide from Ahab through an overt miracle, whereas had Ahab's men discovered him, they would have forced him to revoke the decree, as happened later and as Jehoram did to Elisha.
records.targetHebrew: אכן כשראה אליהו מיתת בן הצרפית, וזאת היה נוגע אצלו עד לחייו, כי אם הילד היתה טוענת שאליהו הוא החייב בדבר בזה שבא להתגורר אצלה וראה הקב"ה מעשיה נגד מעשה אליהו והזכיר את עונה ונענשה, לכן היה נוגע המעשה הזאת לאליהו עד לחייו. והבין מזה שסיבב לו השי"ת מעשה כזאת, שהרצון של השי"ת הוא שיתפלל בעד כל הדור שיחזרו בתשובה, כדי שיהיה מטר אחר שהרעב התגבר כ"כ, לזה היה חפץ השי"ת שיתפלל אליהו בעד כל הדור שיחזרו בתשובה, כי לא יחפוץ השי"ת במות הרשע כי אם בשובו מדרכיו וחיה. וזה כוונת הירושלמי כשהחיה בן הצרפית הותר הנדר של טל ומטר.
